title: Naming pages the way buyers search
metaTitle: Name pages the way buyers search
excerpt: The visible title and the title tag can differ slightly, and both should name the job of the page. Clever names that hide the offer are hard to find and hard to forward.
alt: A hand holding a blue pen over wireframe sketches, with a mug and a closed notebook nearby, a page being named before it is decorated.
caption: A pen over the sketch, while the name is still a decision. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should the title tag match the heading on the page?
faqs.answer: They should describe the same job. The heading can carry a little more of the brand, and the title element can be plainer, with the company name at the end if it still fits. If they describe different offers, readers and search results both get a puzzle, and Google may rewrite the title.

faqs.question: How long should a page title be?
faqs.answer: Short enough to say the job, and specific enough that a founder can paste it into a chat. A unique title per page matters more than hitting a magic character count. Boilerplate that repeats the same slogan on every URL wastes the one line people see in a tab and in a result.

faqs.question: What should you do with internal nicknames?
faqs.answer: Keep nicknames in the repository and in conversation. Put the buyer's words in the navigation, the heading, and the title element. A page called Aurora in the sprint and Solutions on the site will not be found by the person who needs a migration, a pricing shape, or a demo.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Website page titles for search should name the job of the page in words a buyer already uses. The visible heading and the title element can differ a little in tone. They should not differ in offer. A clever name that hides the work will not be found, and it will not survive being pasted into a chat.

Write the name before you decorate the layout. A page with a true name is easy to link, easy to forward, and easier to keep honest as the site grows.

## The heading and the title element

The heading is what a person sees on the page. The title element is what they see in the tab, in the browser history, and often in the search result. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for titles that are descriptive and distinct, and it explains that vague, boilerplate, or misleading titles are the ones Google rewrites. You do not fully control the result line. You do control whether you gave a clear title to start from.

Let the heading be the sentence you want remembered. Let the title element be the plainer version, plus the company name if it still reads as one thought. "Store migration without a broken checkout" on the page, and "Store migration checklist | Hanabi" in the title, is a small and useful difference. "The long way home" on the page, with a title that says "Services," is two different products sharing a URL.

One obvious main heading per page. Several slogans at the same size make the title a guess, and Google's own notes on titles warn about pages where the main point is unclear. Pick the job. Put it in the heading. Do not make the reader, or the result, choose between three moods.

[People-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page has a primary purpose. The title is the purpose, compressed. If you cannot title it, the page may be two pages, or it may be a section that does not deserve a URL. Split or fold it before you invent a poetic compromise.

## Names a buyer would type, and names they would forward

Listen to the words on calls. "We need to move the shop." "We need the homepage to explain the product." "We need a pricing shape." Those phrases are titles waiting to happen. Internal sprint names are not. Aurora, Phoenix, and Northstar can live in the issue tracker. They should not be the navigation.

A forwardable title fits in a message without a preface. "Pricing for teams that need a demo" tells the recipient what they will open. "Our approach" tells them nothing, so they ask you, and you become the documentation. The site's job is to travel without you.

Match the navigation label, the heading, and the title. A nav item that says Work, a heading that says Selected stories, and a title that says Portfolio make people think the link failed. Pick one job name and use it in all three. Small words can change. The offer cannot.

Write the title for the stranger, not for the stakeholder who wanted their initiative visible. A page named after an internal program will rank, if it ranks, for a query nobody types. It will also confuse the buyer who came for the offer. Stakeholder comfort is cheaper to fix in a meeting than in the information architecture.

## A pattern you can keep

Use a pattern so the site does not renegotiate every URL.

- Home: the offer and who it is for.
- A service or product page: the job, not the department.
- Proof: the constraint, not the word Case.
- A doc: the task, such as "Invite a teammate."
- An article: the decision the reader is trying to make.

The company name can sit at the end of the title element, once, so a tab is identifiable. Repeating the name in every heading makes the heading worse. The heading is for the person already on the site. They know where they are. Tell them what this page will do.

Avoid stuffing a chain of synonyms into the title to chase queries. "Web design website design agency design studio" is not a name. It is a tell, and it is exactly the kind of title that gets rewritten or ignored. One job. The real words. If you have a second audience, give them a second page with its own title, rather than a single title that tries to be both.

Keep titles stable when the meaning is stable. Changing them every quarter for freshness breaks bookmarks and breaks the memory of anyone who forwarded the old line. Change a title when the page's job changed. Say so in the changelog if the page is part of a product people rely on.

## On the page, the name has to be true

A precise title over a vague page is a broken promise. The first paragraph should cash the title. If the title says the page is about checkout migration, the first screen should be about checkout migration, with proof that matches. Down the Cove, as an ecommerce migration and redesign, is the kind of proof that belongs under a commerce title. It does not belong under a title about brand films. Neighbors matter. A mismatched proof makes a good title look like bait.

The H1 and the title can be siblings, not clones. Do not hide the H1 and hope the title element does the talking. People on the page need the heading. People in search need the title. Both are readers. Serve both with the same fact.

Breadcrumbs and nav should use the short form of the same name. A breadcrumb that says Resources, when the title says a specific job, throws away the specificity you just earned. If the section is real, name the section after the jobs in it. "Docs" can stay if the pages inside are titled as tasks. "Solutions" rarely earns its keep.

In the product, screen titles are the same problem at a smaller size. "Settings" is a warehouse. "Who can invite a teammate" is a destination. You do not need search-result craft inside an app. You do need names a user can find in their own memory. The vocabulary list from the brand voice should govern both.

## How to review a set of titles

Open every public URL in tabs. Read only the tab labels. You should be able to say what each page is for without switching to it. Duplicates will jump out. Untitled CMS defaults will jump out. So will the page that is still called Home Copy 2.

Then search your own site, if it has search, for a job a buyer would type. See which title comes back. If the right page is missing, or comes back under a name they would not recognize, fix the title and the heading before you add more body copy. More copy under a bad name is a longer miss.

Look at the queries you already receive, in the search console or in the words people use on calls. If a query describes a page you have, and the title does not contain the job in their words, adjust the title toward them without turning it into a list. You are translating, not collecting. One strong phrase beats five weak ones jammed with bars.

Ask a teammate who did not build the site to forward three pages to you, using only the titles. If they have to add a sentence of explanation, the title failed. That test takes ten minutes. It is stricter than a debate about tone, and it is closer to the way the page will actually travel.

## Titles, speed, and the first screen

The title is a promise the first screen has to keep quickly. A heavy hero that delays the heading makes the name arrive late. Treat the heading as content that should paint with the page, not as a caption under a film. Motion can arrive after the name is readable, and it should respect a reduced-motion setting.

On a Next.js site the title element is a piece of the page's metadata, owned in the same place as the route. Do not let a layout template overwrite every child with the company slogan. Set the title beside the page. Review it in code review the way you review a redirect. A wrong title is a defect. It is not a flourish to be cleaned up at the end, because the end is when everyone is tired and the slogan wins.

Share the pattern with whoever edits the CMS. A field labeled "SEO title" that nobody understands will be left blank or stuffed. Label it "Tab and search title. Name the job. Company name is added for you." Defaults prevent the worst blanks. Examples prevent the worst stuffing. Give both.

## The limit of a good name

A clear title cannot rescue a page with nothing to say. It cannot invent demand. It can make a true page findable and forwardable, which is the whole job of a name. If the underlying offer is fuzzy, fix the offer. A sharper title on a foggy promise only helps the wrong people arrive faster, and then leave.

Do not name pages for a ranking you have not earned with the body. The title is a claim that the page must satisfy. [Helpful content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is the standard: a purpose, a reader, something useful if they came for that title. Meet it. Then stop fiddling.

When the titles are honest and the docs are large enough that people will not browse, search inside the docs becomes the next design problem. [Internal search on a documentation site](/blog/internal-search-on-a-documentation-site) is about showing the heading that matched, and giving a failed search somewhere to go. Read it before you hide a weak information architecture behind a search box.

If you want help naming the pages so a stranger can find them and forward them, book [an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current tab labels. The half hour should produce a shorter list of jobs, which is the list of titles.
